Use streaming to improve perceived latency.
Parallelize independent operations and avoid unnecessary sequential LLM calls.
Understand when smaller/faster models can replace larger models.
Apply prompt/context reduction, batching, and inference-service optimizations where appropriate.
Reason about throughput, latency, and utilization at scale.

notes: Inference performance and both model- and service-level optimization are major topics in the book’s inference optimization chapter.
modules.outcome: Identify where an AI application is slow and choose the appropriate optimization instead of simply upgrading infrastructure.

modules.name: Caching architecture

objectives.text: Understand the different caches available in an AI system: exact-response caching, prompt/context caching, retrieval caching, and semantic caching.
Decide what is safe to cache and define appropriate expiration/invalidation strategies.
Use semantic caching when different queries can reasonably share an answer.
Understand the trade-off between freshness, quality, latency, and cost.
Measure actual cache hit rate and savings rather than assuming caching helps.

notes: Caching is another explicit step in Huyen’s production AI architecture.
modules.outcome: Use caching as an architectural optimization rather than an afterthought.

modules.name: Reliability, guardrails & graceful degradation

objectives.text: Design for model failures, provider outages, tool failures, rate limits, malformed outputs, and retrieval failures.
Add timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, queues, and rate limits where appropriate.
Place guardrails at important system boundaries rather than relying entirely on the model.
Design graceful degradation: simpler model, reduced functionality, cached answer, human escalation, or explicit inability to complete the request.
Use human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions.
Define service-level expectations for availability, latency, and quality.

modules.outcome: Design a system that remains useful when individual AI components fail.

modules.name: AI pipeline orchestration

objectives.text: Design the end-to-end flow between retrieval, models, tools, agents, guardrails, caches, and external systems.
Decide which decisions should be deterministic and which should be delegated to the model.
Choose between synchronous execution, asynchronous jobs, queues, and long-running agent workflows.
Avoid unnecessary agentic complexity when a deterministic pipeline is sufficient.
Define clear component boundaries so individual parts can be changed, evaluated, and scaled independently.

notes: Pipeline orchestration and agent patterns both appear explicitly in the book’s final architecture chapter.
modules.outcome: Turn individual AI components into a coherent production system.

modules.name: Monitoring, feedback & continuous improvement

objectives.text: Connect evals, traces, operational metrics, and user feedback into the production architecture.
Monitor quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval behavior, tool usage, and model/provider performance.
Capture explicit feedback such as ratings as well as useful implicit behavioral signals.
Turn production failures and user feedback into new evaluation cases.
Version models, prompts, retrieval configurations, and application changes so regressions can be traced.
Understand the loop: deploy → observe → collect feedback → evaluate → improve → redeploy.

notes: Huyen’s final chapter explicitly treats monitoring/observability and user-feedback design as parts of the AI engineering architecture.
modules.outcome: Design AI products that improve from real-world usage rather than remaining static after launch.

modules.name: AI system design case studies

objectives.text: Whiteboard several systems end-to-end and defend the choices.
Design around:
RAG and fresh knowledge,
citations,
model routing,
caching,
escalation to humans,
latency and cost constraints.
Design around:
large codebase context,
retrieval,
tool/code execution,
model selection,
sandboxing,
long-running tasks.
Design around:
search and retrieval,
planning,
parallel tool calls,
context management,
long-running execution,
citations,
cost budgets and failure recovery.
For each case, reason about requirements → baseline → architecture → bottlenecks → failure modes → scaling → trade-offs.

modules.outcome: Defend architectural decisions rather than merely draw boxes and arrows.

modules.name: Capstone: AI System Design Document

objectives.text: Choose a substantial AI product and produce a complete design covering:
requirements and success criteria,
expected traffic and constraints,
high-level architecture,
model choice and routing,
context/RAG architecture,
tools/agents where required,
caching strategy,
latency and cost budget,
reliability and fallback strategy,
security/guardrails,
evaluation and monitoring,
user-feedback loop,
scaling strategy.
Include an architecture diagram and explicitly justify the major trade-offs and alternatives rejected.

modules.finalResult: a design you could defend in an AI system-design interview or an engineering architecture review.

completionOutcomes: Translate product requirements into an AI system architecture.
Decide between prompting, RAG, agents, and fine-tuning.
Design context and retrieval architecture.
Build model routing, gateways, cascades, and fallbacks.
Optimize inference for latency, throughput, and cost.
Design appropriate caching layers.
Build for failures and graceful degradation.
Decide what should be deterministic versus agentic.
Integrate monitoring, evals, and user feedback into the architecture.
Reason about the entire application rather than optimizing individual AI components in isolation.
Whiteboard and defend a production AI system end-to-end.

levels.title: LLMOps: From Development to Production
levels.scope: Launch, test, watch, and protect Large Language Model apps in the real world while managing changing outputs, prompt updates, and the special behaviors of RAG and Agent systems.

modules.name: Foundations of LLMOps

objectives.text: Define exactly what LLMOps is: the organized process of building, testing, watching, and running Large Language Model applications in the real world.
Explain why LLMOps is its own special field and how it is different from regular MLOps.
Compare Model LLMOps (which means training, fine-tuning, and hosting raw AI models) with Application LLMOps (which means building and running useful apps on top of existing AI models).

Look at the Model LLMOps lifecycle—gathering huge amounts of data, updating model weights, and managing massive servers—and understand why we chose to focus on Application LLMOps instead, since most teams today build apps rather than make their own models from scratch.
Map the complete journey of an LLM app from early building stages to putting it live and watching its performance.
Show how the daily running of a RAG app is different from an Agentic app.
Give a big-picture view of the whole LLMOps toolkit, including how we access models, check quality, track errors, keep things safe, and update code automatically.
Understand the two main projects (a RAG app and an Agentic app) that we will build and manage during this course.

modules.outcome: Understand the full journey of an LLM application and the complete LLMOps toolkit before writing any code.

modules.name: Application development

objectives.text: Build a RAG app that reads documents, breaks them into pieces, stores them, and connects them to an LLM to answer questions.
Build an Agent app that uses tools, plans steps, remembers past actions, and works on its own.
Use basic tools like LangChain for RAG, LangGraph for Agents, Chroma for storage, and OpenAI or Anthropic models.

modules.outcome: Set up the basic RAG and Agent apps that we will improve and put online in later steps.

modules.name: Evaluation

objectives.text: Create test question-answer pairs automatically using DeepEval instead of typing them out by hand.
Run a full test on both apps and save the starting scores in MLflow before changing any code.
Score the RAG app on how truthful and exact it is using AI-as-a-judge tools.
Score the Agent app on whether it picks the right tools, finishes the job, and takes logical steps.
Set up automatic alarms to catch if new changes break the app.

modules.outcome: Measure the quality of your LLM apps automatically without needing humans to check every answer.

modules.name: Experiment tracking & prompt versioning

objectives.text: Save and manage different versions of prompts using Langfuse so apps can pull them when running.
Label prompt versions for different stages like testing and live production.
Keep track of RAG settings (like chunk size) and Agent settings (like tools) as recorded MLflow experiments.
Track Metrics and artifacts along with the parameters.
Compare different prompt versions side-by-side in a dashboard to see how changes affect the output.

modules.outcome: Keep a clear, organized history of your prompts and app settings so you can easily repeat success.

modules.name: Guardrails & output safety

objectives.text: Look at different safety tools like Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails
Force the LLM to give answers in a strict format and automatically ask again if it gets it wrong using Guardrails AI.
Add checkers to block bad user inputs and stop prompt injection attacks.
Add checkers to stop the LLM from making things up, going off-topic, or leaking private data.
Put strict limits on Agent apps to check tool inputs and stop the agent from getting stuck in endless loops.

modules.outcome: Check and fix inputs and outputs to make sure the LLM app is safe and reliable before users see the results.

modules.name: Application serving & containerization

objectives.text: Move the app logic from simple scripts into a strong, real-world FastAPI backend.
Turn Streamlit into just a screen that talks to the FastAPI backend.
Send answers word-by-word in real time (streaming) so users do not have to wait for the whole reply.
Create an application frontend using Streamlit which handles user queries
Pack the frontend and backend into Docker containers and connect them using Docker Compose.
Hide passwords and API keys safely inside the containers using .env files.

modules.outcome: Upgrade the apps into a fast, streaming, and easily movable container setup.

modules.name: CI/CD with GitHub Actions

objectives.text: Build automatic pipelines in GitHub Actions that use your tests as a strict door to production.
Run the DeepEval tests automatically every time you push new code.
Stop the release instantly if any test score falls below your set limits.
Build effective gates to apply regression testing on new versions
Build Docker images with clear version tags only after all tests pass.
Upload the safe and tested Docker images to Docker Hub.

modules.outcome: Automate your testing and building steps so only high-quality code goes live.

modules.name: Deployment on AWS

objectives.text: Set up AWS EC2 servers to run LLM workloads, installing Docker and the right access roles.
Automate the release process using AWS CodeDeploy to pull new Docker images and swap them safely.
Set up a Load Balancer to manage traffic and make sure the word-by-word streaming works smoothly.
Add Auto Scaling to automatically add more servers when busy and remove them when quiet.
Store sensitive API keys securely in the cloud using AWS Secrets Manager.

modules.outcome: Launch your packed apps on AWS with automatic updates, traffic management, and scaling.

modules.name: Post-deployment monitoring

objectives.text: Set up Prometheus on a special server to gather health data from all your running machines.
Watch computer health stats like CPU, memory, and network usage using Node Exporter.
Track app stats like the number of requests, LLM calls, and tokens used.
Build simple Grafana dashboards to see the health of your servers, app traffic, and LLM behavior in one place.
Set up alarms in Grafana to warn you if servers get too busy or fail to scale.
Monitor logs, latency and token costs for each of your inputs through tracing.
Run frequent online evaluations over your app.

modules.outcome: Keep a close watch on your live AWS setup, covering both the computer health and app speed.

modules.name: Capstone: LLMOps Project

objectives.text: Choose an Agent app and show off the whole LLMOps process from start to finish.
Build around core LLMOps steps: app building, tracking settings, automatic testing, live watching, safety checkers, Docker packing, auto-releases, AWS hosting, and Grafana dashboards.
For this project, follow the path: build →  test → track → secure → pack → launch → watch.

modules.outcome: Show a fully launched, watched, and safe Agent app built from the ground up.

completionOutcomes: Build LLM apps and move them into real-world container setups.
Manage different prompt versions and track settings easily.
Test RAG and Agent apps thoroughly without needing perfect human answers.
Force exact output formats and block bad inputs or data leaks.
Make automatic pipelines that test your app before letting it go live.
Launch, balance traffic, and automatically grow your LLM servers on AWS.
Watch your instance health, app speed, and LLM costs continuously in the real world.

levels.title: Advanced AI Systems (Multimodal)
levels.scope: work across modalities and at the current shippable frontier.

objectives.text: Explain, intuitively, how multimodal models fuse text with other modalities.
Do image Q&A and document/PDF understanding, including charts and tables.
Build visual RAG.
Build speech-to-text (Whisper) and text-to-speech (Kokoro) pipelines.
Use a realtime API with turn-taking, interruption, and low latency.
Use generation models and controllable-generation techniques.
Build long-horizon research and synthesis into structured reports.
Run small quantized models locally and reason about the tradeoffs.

objectives.text: Ship one end-to-end multimodal build.

Measure before/after on Level-8 evals and catch regressions.

objectives.text: Connect a model to a calendar/CRM/task manager — the 2026 pattern.
